title: Fake News? Quantifying the Prevalence of Misinformation Related to Scoliosis on the TikTok Social Media Platform
screen_reason: Content analysis of 239 TikTok videos found under five scoliosis hashtags (20-27 December 2022). Videos offering medical advice were flagged and reviewed by three fellowship-trained pediatric spine-deformity surgeons who marked their content supported or unsupported by current medical evidence; 44% (24/55) of advice videos contained misinformation. That is a share of items judged inaccurate against expert/evidence ground truth, so CONTENT. The GQS and DISCERN quality instruments are reported as means only and therefore yield no row.

estimates.date: 20-27 December 2022 (all five hashtags collected within a 7-day period)
estimates.measure_type: % of scoliosis TikTok videos offering medical advice or treatment information that contained misinformation on expert review
estimates.value_raw: 44% (n = 24) of 55 videos providing medical advice or treatment information
estimates.denominator: 55 videos that provided medical advice, discussed treatment options or attempted to educate the public about scoliosis, flagged out of the 239 videos reviewed under #scoliosis, #scoliosischiropractor, #scoliosisbrace and #scoliosissurgery (plus #scoliosissurgeon)
estimates.definition: Flagged video judged by three fellowship-trained pediatric orthopaedic spine-deformity surgeons as NOT supported by current medical evidence ('marked them as either supported or unsupported')
estimates.misinfo_def: No verbal definition; operationalised as content not 'supported by current medical evidence' per expert surgeon review. The paper adds that 'The most common misinformation topics included misconceptions about scoliosis surgery, bracing effectiveness, and scoliosis progression.'

estimates.page_loc: p. 3, Results (final Results paragraph); repeated in Abstract and Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-stage: three authors with clinical research experience (A.D., M.M., E.L.) watched the first 50 videos together to calibrate categorisation, then coded independently, flagging any video giving medical advice or education; flagged videos were then adjudicated by three fellowship-trained pediatric orthopaedic surgeons specialising in spine deformity against current medical evidence. No inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported for either stage, and it is not stated how surgeon disagreements were resolved.
estimates.moderator_quote: Between December 20, 2022, and December 27, 2022, a comprehensive search was conducted on the TikTok social media platform using the following hashtags: #scoliosis, #scoliosischiropractor, #scoliosisbrace, #scoliosisbrace, and #scoliosissurgery. ... Any video that provided medical advice, discussed treatment options or attempted to educate the public about scoliosis was flagged for further review. These flagged videos were assessed by three fellowship-trained pediatric orthopaedic surgeons specializing in spine deformity, who reviewed them to determine whether the content was supported by current medical evidence and marked them as either supported or unsupported.
estimates.notes: DENOMINATOR MATTERS: 44% is the share among ADVICE videos only (55 of 239). The remaining 184 videos - overwhelmingly patient-experience posts (72.8% of all videos were patient experiences) - were never assessed for veracity, so the whole-corpus figure 24/239 = 10.0% would be a floor, not an equivalent estimate; it is not made a row because those 184 videos are unassessed rather than assessed-and-clean. breadth coded 'misleading' because the criterion is 'not supported by current medical evidence', which is broader than demonstrably false. The hashtag set is inconsistently reported (#scoliosisbrace is listed twice in Methods; Table 3 and Table 4 show five hashtags including #Scoliosis Surgeon). See missed_or_uncertain for arithmetic errors in Table 4 that an adjudicator should be aware of - they do not affect this row's value, which is stated identically three times.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) TABLE 4 IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT and no row was built from it. Its 'Misinformation YES' column by hashtag sums to 24 (7+11+1+0+5), matching the text, but the 'Misinformation No' column sums to 30, not 31. By author type the YES column reads Medical Doctor 3, Chiropractor 12, Nurse 2, Patient 165 - summing to 182, impossible when only 24 videos contain misinformation; the 'Patient 165 (91.2%)' cell is plainly a typo, and the chiropractor count (12) contradicts the text and abstract (11, 45.8%). Percentages in the same rows are computed on different bases again (e.g. Medical Doctor '3 (20%)' of 15 physician videos vs the text's '12.5%, n = 3' of the 24 misinformation videos). (2) Provider subgroup shares of misinformation (chiropractors 45.8% n=11, physicians 12.5% n=3 of the 24 misinformation videos) are shares of the numerator, not prevalence rates, and are subgroup breakdowns, so no rows. (3) GQS (mean 2.5, range 1-5) and DISCERN (mean 2.1) are quality scales reported as MEANS only with no share of videos below any threshold, so per the instructions no QUALITY row is created; the same applies to the by-hashtag and by-author-type quality means. (4) View counts by misinformation status are means with huge SDs (2.2M +/- 5.2M vs 1.6M +/- 5.1M, P = .7), not shares, so no EXPOSURE row is possible - the paper never reports what share of total views went to misinformation videos. (5) Author-type shares (72.8% patient experiences, 74.9% non-HCP, chiropractors 16.3%, physicians 5.9%) describe who posts, not veracity. (6) No CONCENTRATION statistic is reported. (7) Introduction figures (80% of 18-49s seeking health information on social media, 84% Facebook, 53% YouTube, 73% of Gen-Z on TikTok, 47% of POSNA members) are cited from other sources and excluded per R8.

rob.design: Level IV cross-sectional content analysis. Frame: a search of all TikTok hashtags containing 'scoliosis', from which the five hashtags with the most videos were selected; 239 videos reviewed over a single 7-day window (20-27 December 2022), each hashtag collected in one session to hold engagement metrics stable, using new logins on company devices to limit algorithmic personalisation. Three trained reviewers calibrated on the first 50 videos jointly then coded independently (tone, author type, HCP type, educational vs experiential); advice/educational videos were flagged and adjudicated for evidence support by three fellowship-trained pediatric spine surgeons. No inter-rater reliability statistics are reported at either stage, no protocol for surgeon disagreement is described, the number of videos per hashtag is uneven (50/38/44/46/46 in Table 3, total 224, not 239), and Table 4's misinformation counts contain arithmetic errors. Quality scored with GQS and an adapted binary five-item DISCERN; analyses by independent-samples t-tests in Excel/SPSS.
